sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Disaster recovery defines how much data and downtime an organization can tolerate, measures system reliability and repair time, prepares alternate sites and redundant systems, and verifies that recovery plans work.
sections.callout: MEASURE → PREPARE → FAIL OVER → RECOVER → TEST

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: Given an outage or disaster, identify whether the requirement concerns acceptable data loss, acceptable downtime, reliability, repair time, alternate-site readiness, redundancy behavior, or testing.
bullets: How much data can we lose? → RPO
How long can we be down? → RTO
How long does repair take? → MTTR
One active and one waiting → Active-passive

sections.title: Disaster Recovery Metrics

entries.title: Recovery Point Objective (RPO)
paragraphs: RPO defines the maximum acceptable data loss measured backward in time. A four-hour RPO means backup and recovery design should normally prevent losing more than about four hours of data.
entries.recognitionCue: We can lose no more than 30 minutes of data → RPO.

entries.title: Recovery Time Objective (RTO)
paragraphs: RTO is the target time allowed to restore a service after disruption. A two-hour RTO means the recovery design should return the service within that target.
entries.recognitionCue: The application must operate again within one hour → RTO.

entries.title: Mean Time to Repair (MTTR)
paragraphs: MTTR is the average time required to repair or restore a failed component or system. Lower MTTR means faster average recovery.
entries.memoryHook: It broke; how long until it is fixed?

entries.title: Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF)
paragraphs: MTBF is the average operating time between failures of a repairable component. Higher MTBF generally indicates greater reliability.
entries.memoryHook: How long does it run before failing again?

sections.callout: Data loss → RPO. Downtime target → RTO. Repair duration → MTTR. Reliability/time between failures → MTBF.

sections.title: Cold, Warm, and Hot Sites

entries.title: Cold Site
paragraphs: A cold site is the least prepared alternate facility. It may have space and basic infrastructure but requires substantial equipment, data, configuration, and setup before work can resume. It generally costs less but recovers more slowly.
entries.memoryHook: Build it when you get there.

entries.title: Warm Site
paragraphs: A warm site is partially prepared. Infrastructure and some equipment may exist, but data restoration, configuration, or other work remains before full operation.

entries.title: Hot Site
paragraphs: A hot site maintains systems and infrastructure close to operational readiness for rapid resumption. It recovers fastest but generally costs the most.

sections.callout: Cold → Build. Warm → Finish. Hot → Go.

sections.title: High-Availability Approaches

entries.title: Active-Active
paragraphs: In active-active, multiple systems serve production traffic at the same time. If one fails, the remaining active systems continue handling requests.

entries.title: Active-Passive
paragraphs: In active-passive, one system provides service while another waits on standby to take over after failure.

sections.callout: Work + work → Active-active. Work + wait → Active-passive.

sections.title: Disaster Recovery Testing
paragraphs: An untested recovery plan may fail during a real disaster. Testing identifies missing assumptions, unclear responsibilities, and nonfunctional recovery steps.

entries.title: Tabletop Exercise
paragraphs: Participants discuss and walk through a disaster scenario, responsibilities, response steps, and likely problems without necessarily causing a production failover.

entries.title: Validation Test
paragraphs: A validation test verifies that recovery procedures, systems, and capabilities actually function as expected.

sections.callout: Discuss the response → Tabletop. Verify the capability → Validation.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Primary serving and secondary waiting → Active-passive

entries.title: RPO vs. RTO
paragraphs: How much data can we lose? → RPO. How long can we be down? → RTO.

entries.title: RTO vs. MTTR
paragraphs: RTO is the recovery target or requirement. MTTR is the observed average repair or restoration duration.

entries.title: MTTR vs. MTBF
paragraphs: Repair duration → MTTR. Reliability and time between failures → MTBF.

entries.title: Cold vs. Warm vs. Hot
paragraphs: Minimal readiness → Cold. Partial readiness → Warm. High readiness → Hot.

entries.title: Active-Active vs. Active-Passive
paragraphs: Both systems serve → Active-active. One serves while one waits → Active-passive.

entries.title: Tabletop vs. Validation
paragraphs: Discuss the response → Tabletop. Verify recovery capability → Validation.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: One works and one waits → Active-passive
sections.callout: MEASURE → PREPARE → FAIL OVER → RECOVER → TEST
